newsitem.title: USA: FBI probes Gingrich tape leak; Democrat steps down.
newsitem.headline: FBI probes Gingrich tape leak; Democrat steps down.

text.p: FBI Director Louis Freeh said on Tuesday he had ordered an immediate investigation into the taping and leaking of a telephone conference call between House Speaker Newt Gingrich and his top lieutenants.

Freeh's announcement came as the House ethics committee's top Democrat, Representative Jim McDermott of Washington, who was at the centre of the tape furore, announced conditionally he would step aside from consideration of the Gingrich ethics case.
Freeh said the investigation would look into "a possible illegal telephone interception and the subsequent dissemination of the contents of the telephone call."

In a letter to Representative Henry Hyde, R-Illinois, who had demanded an investigation, Freeh said, "The opening of this investigation should not be interpreted as conclusive that there were in fact violations of the law."

McDermott received on Wednesday the tape of the conference call between Gingrich and his top lieutenants, two days before transcripts of it appeared in the press. It was now in the custody of the Justice Department.

In a statement that blasted the way the committee has been run by the Republican chairman, Representative Nancy Johnson of Connecticut, McDermott set a caveat on his "recusal" from the Gingrich case, saying it was conditional on steps being taken to preserve the panel's equal ratio between the parties.
The committee is divided five-five between Republicans and Democrats, including a Republican who joined the committee in recentl weeks as a replacement solely for consideration of the Gingrich case.

The furore over the leaked tape was just one of a series of controversies in the committee that has created an atmosphere of bitter partisanship just as the new Republican-controlled Congress was getting under way amid talk of cooperation.

McDermott was given the tape by a Florida couple who monitored the cellular phone conversation on a police scanner while driving near Jacksonville. When they recognised the voices they taped the conversation.
They told a news conference on Monday they gave the tape to Representative Karen Thurman, D-Florida, and then passed it to McDermott on Thurman's advice while visiting Congress.

Republicans demanded a criminal investigation and a member of the Republican leadership team, Representative Bill Paxon of New York, demanded on Tuesday that Democrats "come clean" about the affair. He said he and others taking part in the eavesdropped call were considering civil suit for damages.

Democrats responded with an attack on Johnson, introducing a House resolution condemning her for unilaterally scrapping a plan adopted by the committee that called for up to five days of public hearings on the Gingrich ethics case this week.
McDermott, who is winding up six years' service on the ethics committee, declared in a statement: "I no longer can participate in this charade."
He said that on Monday night Johnson refused to place before the committee "evidence relevent to determining whether or not the speaker intentionally lied about his conduct."

Gingrich has admitted giving the committee false information but said it was unintentional. He also admitted failing to seek legal advice to ensure that charitable contributions were not used for political purposes in college courses he taught.
McDermott said committee Republicans had "delayed, stonewalled, or otherwise obstructed sensible efforts to get at the truth."

Johnson responded in a two-sentence statement that she would not allow "angry partisanship" to divert the committee from its job and the panel was moving towards full disclosure and a hearing on the Gingrich case.

Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt, reacting to McDermott's decision to remove himself from the Gingrich case, said it was made in the interests of the committee and the public's right to hear the facts "without distraction."
